This study introduces a novel time-changing Poisson autoregressive model, incorporating a random effects specification to account for non-constant variance and non-linearity in the data-generating process. We demonstrate the efficacy of our conditional heteroscedastic and time-varying variance model by applying it to forecasting daily electricity consumption, replacing a traditional constant variance model. Our findings indicate that the proposed approach yields significant improvements in forecast accuracy, measured by the mean absolute percentage error, compared to the standard time-changing heteroscedastic model and a popular benchmark model.

While using photometry from space-based telescopes to monitor aerosols in the atmosphere may seem straightforward, various complexities and sources of error arise when analyzing the resulting data. A major challenge in this method is accurately determining the amount of aerosol-induced scattering of light by the atmosphere, which can be achieved by comparing observed and calculated stellar fluxes. Currently, this assessment relies on sophisticated models that account for atmospheric conditions, a system that may soon be enhanced by a new constellation of telescopes scheduled for launch in the mid-2020s. Although this new constellation is expected to provide significant benefits, including a larger array of telescopes and a shorter wavelength range, it will also introduce novel challenges and sources of error. In response to these anticipated developments, we have implemented a novel approach based on a physical parameter that directly links aerosol properties and observable stellar fluxes, minimizing the influence of atmospheric gas absorption and aerosol type. As a result, we believe that this new technique will be particularly valuable for the upcoming telescope mission, which is set to launch in 2028, although it may also be applicable to current and future space-based photometry initiatives.

Numerous configurational molecular sampling methods in molecular dynamics simulations are based on Brownian dynamics or Langevin dynamics, which rely on random numbers to guide motion. However, the fixed seed for random numbers across multiple configurations can lead to the same molecular configuration being visited multiple times, decreasing the efficiency of these methods. Additionally, this issue can cause different initial conditions to yield different outcomes when using these methods, particularly when mapping them onto deterministic Newtonian dynamics. Here, we demonstrate that this problem is not unique to random number generation but rather stems from the fixed seed being passed directly to the molecular configuration. We present a novel approach where we use a hash function to map distinct initial conditions onto the same random number seed, showing that using the most significant bit of the hash value offers improved performance compared to using the random number itself. We also explore alternative implementations, such as using the most significant bits of the input parameters, and find that they yield similar results. Furthermore, we observe that using the most significant bit of the hash function of the molecular configuration itself offers the best performance in our experiments, metastable protein conformation changes, and protein-ligand binding, without requiring additional computational expense.

Recent advances in image description techniques have been outpaced by the growth of images on the internet, prompting the development of methods that generate text summarizing pictures. Although these methods show promise, evaluating their effectiveness and comparing different approaches can be challenging and controversial. This dispute arose recently between two studies that drew opposite conclusions about the reliability of human feedback in assessing image description quality. The first study suggested that human feedback may be inaccurate and unhelpful, whereas the second study found it to be valuable and useful. This paper aims to investigate these findings, explore the underlying reasons, and provide a clearer understanding of the strengths and limitations of human feedback. It also introduces a novel, more precise metric called "Describable Events Dataset" (DED) and utilized three widely used images (natural scenes) as a case study to demonstrate the effectiveness of human feedback in evaluating image description quality. The results showed that human feedback correlates strongly with the proposed metric and improves image description performance when combined with existing evaluation methods. Consequently, the research advises utilizing human feedback in conjunction with visually grounded similarities when assessing image description quality and conducting manual evaluations to calibrate the performance of image description models.

A geometric theory combining physics and field physics was explored for consistency checks. Based on a previous approach by Kerstien and Weinstock, a consistency check between the equation of motion and the conservation law was achieved. The method involves comparing the Lie derivative of a physical field phase space distribution to its equation of motion. An application of the method resulted in a new equation of motion for chiral Wess-Scherrer models. Furthermore, the method revealed a hidden topological conservation law in a specific model.

Predictions from extra dimension theories that eliminate normal matter's lightness may foretell the discovery of unusual baryons and mesons. Since these predictions are based on eliminated scale symmetry restoration, understanding its impact on quark masses is crucial. This involves recognizing how asymptotic freedom affects scale symmetry breaking and how it is reflected in heavy quark effective theories. Lambshifts and hyperfine splittings of baryons and mesons can be predicted by calculating how eliminated scale symmetry affects asymptotic freedom. This knowledge can also inform researchers about potential new physics that might manifest as unseen baryons and mesons.
This article presents SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM equivalents for the broadband waveforming strategy outlined in our prior research, which focuses on combining data and power transfer via IFDT.

We have developed a comprehensive framework that integrates various particle production processes, allows for the simultaneous modification of different partons as a result of non-perturbative phase space splittings, and accounts for (anti-)quark annihilation contributions. This framework's key component, a 2-dimensional matrix $M$, enables the calculation of (anti-)quark or gluon distribution functions that have been altered by such processes. The matrix $M$ can be diagonalized to obtain the eigenvalues, which represent the shifts in the (anti-)quark or gluon distribution functions. We have also derived an analytical formula for the adjusted (anti-)quark or gluon distribution function, based on the eigenvalues' values and their corresponding eigenfunctions. This formula serves as the foundation for creating customized (anti-)quark or gluon distribution functions for use in Monte Carlo simulations.

This study investigates the acoustic excitation of a turbulent jet fire in a linearized stability framework using an active flame model. Contrary to previous research, we utilize a approach that accounts for flame-response functions to acoustic signals. A computational model is employed to simulate the jet fire, with the reaction rates determined based on the stability characteristics of the flame. We use a simplified chemistry model, assuming a single reaction rate constant. The simulation parameters are validated using existing data on a steady laminar flame. We then conduct multiple simulations to examine the reaction rates and heat-release rates in response to acoustic excitation, with varying amplitudes and frequencies. The results show that the reaction rates correlate with the flame-response functions, with higher rates exhibited near the flame root for larger amplitude signals. We also observe varying heat-release pattern outcomes based on signal frequency.

Nonlocal gravitation theory seeks to link gravity with mass and energy through a fourth vector field, as both a fundamental force and a response to one. A key aspect of this approach is the way this vector field interacts with the underlying structure of spacetime, specifically with tetrads that define gravity at a given point. A widely accepted method for integrating this vector field into the nonlocal gravity framework involves using a constitutive relation, which in this case is given by a Poiseuille model. We demonstrate that this particular constitutive relation is universally applicable for all nonlocal gravity theories, as well as all massless scalar fields, by incorporating the underlying structure of spacetime into the theory. A notable outcome of this integration is the direct link between the gravitational force and its underlying causes, providing a fundamental understanding of gravity as a response to mass and energy within the nonlocal gravity framework.

This paper discusses recent findings from the LHC involving tiny systems, which are examined through fixed-target and polarized-beam collisions. The research focuses on determining the properties of low-mass states, particularly the axion-like pseudoscalars, and understanding their connection to tiny systems. The results of searches for compositeness, contact interactions, and ComCom physics are presented, as well as the investigation of form factor measurements and the analysis of tiny systems in polarized proton collisions. The research also examines recent findings from the LHC involving tiny systems in polarized proton collisions and the potential for future polarized proton colliders to study these systems. The paper concludes by discussing the theoretical background for tiny systems in proton-proton collisions and the importance of understanding missing transverse momentum in tiny system research.

Observations of some neutron star X-ray binary transients have revealed unusual recurrence patterns, prompting a re-examination of existing data. By re-evaluating the recurrence intervals of six previously misunderstood or under-reviewed sources, we've established that at least three of them exhibit long interburst periods following a first outburst. This counter-intuitive behavior challenges the widely accepted idea that short recurrence intervals signal an accretion-powered millisecond X-ray binary with a low-mass neutron star. An alternative explanation, supported by theoretical models, suggests that these binaries with long interburst periods might actually contain an intermediate-mass companion star. This discovery opens the possibility that many unspotted or poorly resolved X-ray sources within the Galactic Centre may also have intermediate-mass companions, potentially revolutionizing our understanding of the binary population in crowded star clusters by revealing a previously hidden class of low-luminosity binaries.

Given a bipartite graph B = (U $\cup$ V, E), the Bipartite Vertex Partition problem seeks the minimum number of parts into which nodes in U or V can be divided such that fully connected components are formed. A previous algorithm solved this problem in O(3.276^n) time, whereas the currently suggested algorithm takes FPT time in relation to the parameter k.

As CPU frequencies continue to increase, there's a growing concern about energy efficiency, particularly in low-power cores. To address this challenge, a new concept of "degradeable" CPU designs has emerged, which intentionally slow down high-performance cores to balance performance and power consumption. Building upon this idea, our HyperDegrade design proposes a novel architecture that gradates CPU frequencies across multiple cores, with a low-power core operating at a slower rate and a high-performance core at a faster rate, versus the standard approach. With Gaussian elimination-based instruction scheduling, HyperDegrade can execute instructions at varying frequencies, allowing for a wide range of performance choices. By varying the frequency ratio between the two cores, we can optimize performance versus energy consumption, achieving a maximum performance improvement of 2.5x with minimal additional area overhead. Furthermore, our design can be fabricated using existing foundries with negligible additional cost. Through evaluation on a variety of workloads, HyperDegrade demonstrates outstanding performance versus energy consumption tradeoffs, outperforming existing degradeable designs by an order of magnitude in some cases, without sacrificing overall CPU frequency.

We present a new algorithm that utilizes a rotation of our knot for unknotting traditional and welded knots, leaving the knot structure unchanged. This process contrasts with existing methods that modify the knot diagram by drawing additional lines. Our approach builds upon a rotation of the knot projectively, which we believe has interesting applications in projective space. The algorithm is straightforward to implement, as it simply involves drawing more lines on the knot diagram, which can then be easily removed to reveal the unknotting path.

In complex environments with numerous obstacles, executing sophisticated tasks with swarms of robots is challenging. This challenge stems from the limitations of robot computation and communication capabilities, which are further constrained when using conventional networks. To address this challenge, a new strategy called "tactical collaboration" has been proposed, where robots use simple actions to convey information about their intentions. This approach enables robots to carry out challenging tasks by forming collaborative strategies and making informed decisions about when to share their intentions with each other. A key aspect of this method is that robots only share their intentions with those that can use the information most effectively, reducing the burden on limited communication resources. This approach has several benefits over existing tactics, as it allows robots to learn from each other, engage in reciprocal helping behaviors, and even participate in competitive interactions to achieve the best outcome. In addition to outlining a viable tactic for robot collaboration, this research also provides a framework for determining the most effective way to share intentions with other robots, which is critical for optimizing complex tasks with swarms of robots with limited capabilities.

We extend Cartesian decomposition technique to groups, by showing that any group can be embedded into a product of finite groups in infinitely many distinct ways, mirroring previous results for coils and bands.

Optical interferometers at the heart of ground-based gravitational wave detectors experience degradation in performance at high frequencies, mainly due to optical noise from suspension losses. A novel configuration called the sloshing-Sagnac topology is proposed to address this issue. By incorporating a recirculating beam that enters the optical cavity from the side, this design surpasses the traditional Michelson layout by eliminating the effects of angular misalignment and optimizing the signal-to-noise ratio. Additionally, this design allows for the compensation of non-idealities caused by non-zero incident angles, which is crucial for achieving high frequency sensitivity. Theoretical modeling indicates that the sloshing-Sagnac layout can outperform the conventional design by a significant margin in sensitivity at high frequencies, with minimal loss in low frequency sensitivity. Consequently, this new design presents a promising solution for improving the sensitivity of future gravitational wave detectors, particularly at high frequencies.

Recent large-scale MIMO systems using stochastic access protocols have a promising future for widespread deployment. With a high number of antennas, the visibility zone in such systems is increasingly complex, even when considering only non-overlapping visibility areas. In determining the optimal transmission strategy, it is crucial to fully comprehend the structure of these non-overlapping visibility zones. A key aspect of this is the lack of overlap between visibility zones of adjacent cells, a claim disputed by the author. The primary contribution of this research is a detailed, geometric explanation for the non-overlapping characteristic of visibility zones in XL-MIMO systems. This explanation is achieved through the construction of a two-dimensional grid representing visibility zone boundaries, with clear implications for cell layout optimization.

Neural network-based language models have revolutionized language generation, particularly in interactive dialog systems, by enabling accurate predictions of user inputs. However, the massive size of these models and the costs associated with training them have sparked concerns and inspired research into more efficient models. In response, $n$-gram based models experienced a resurgence in interest due to their simplicity and effectiveness in filling the gap between small neural models and larger contextual models like transformer models. Building on this momentum, our research introduces a novel approach where a neural language model serves as a learning guide for a $n$-gram based model, enabling the $n$-gram model to learn from a significantly smaller dataset with better performance. Our findings demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms traditional $n$-gram models and even approaches the performance of large neural models in multiple benchmarks. Furthermore, our research presents a practical framework for implementing $n$-gram models in dialog systems, as demonstrated by our promising experimental results showing that our $n$-gram model achieves higher accuracy than a popular neural model in predicting user inputs in a publicly available dataset.

This investigation seeks to examine the potential inaccuracies in ballot tabulation systems, specifically in an artificial setup mimicking a close local election, by introducing errors in vote tabulations and comparing automated optical symbol recognition technology to quick count methods used by news organizations. A combination of statistics and machine learning approaches was employed to correct the inaccuracies, with the quick count method demonstrating superior accuracy in this instance.

This study employs a simple computer model to investigate how planetary rotation and temperature differences affect atmospheric circulation patterns on various planets. Contrary to traditional assumptions, the research reveals that atmospheric circulation on planets with rapid rotation is not necessarily driven by heat distribution at the equator, and that factors like rotation rate, height, and temperature profiles influence the formation of jet streams. Notably, a phenomenon called "turbulent geostrophic circulation" observed on gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn cannot be explained by this particular model, highlighting the need for future research using more complex models that incorporate factors such as atmospheric depth and oceanic circulation.

We provide closed-form integral representations of the reciprocal gamma function, rationalized with quadratic and cubic numerators, as well as a higher-order representation that serves the purpose by removing singularities.

We have adapted the previous work by Marini, Abbritti, Fabbri, and Francaviglia to create a hydrodynamic theory that simulates the behavior of interacting Bose fluids within an uncertain, many-body framework. This new approach abandoned the assumption that the theory is equivalent to secondQuantization, allowing us to bypass the debate over the equivalence of these two concepts. The resulting description of the fluid's dynamics is comprised of an infinite number of coupled equations, which we have shown can be truncated and simplified by assuming the fluid is in a steady-state condition, as initially proposed by Bogoliubov. The resulting dynamics of the theory are divided into two parts: a wave dynamics component that mimics the behavior of phonons within the fluid, and a thermalization component that represents the interaction of phonons with each other and the vacuum. We have further simplified the equation for the wave dynamics phase by eliminating the equation for the quantum flux density, which is not essential for describing the dynamics of the waves within the phase. The resulting description of the wave dynamics is comparable to the previous phonon picture, but with several key improvements: the inclusion of phonon creation and annihilation, the ability to accurately calculate the phonon frequency, and the capability to simulate complex dynamics within confined systems by applying the Wigner function within a Monte Carlo simulation framework.

This systematic review delves into the Instructor-Pupil framework, a promising approach that combines knowledge enhancement and classification, with potential applications in bioinformatics and genomic data analysis. Theoretical foundations, practical considerations, and notable achievements of the Instructor-Pupil framework are examined and presented in a structured manner. A concise overview of the framework's key aspects, both conceptual and tangible, is provided to serve as a foundation for future research and development.

We introduce a new algorithm that uses a brief summary of a function, as opposed to the function itself, to compute the exact Maximum Probability Estimate and perform limited optimization in graphical models. Our method significantly reduces the computational requirements compared to existing methods by using a compact representation of the function that is essentially a small set of its most critical points. We demonstrate that in many cases, our method achieves faster computation times for exact MPE by using the brief summary, and larger optimization spaces when using the gradient, when compared to the current state of the art that utilizes the function itself. Our results indicate that our approach allows for the computation of exact MPE in models with larger optimization spaces and more complex functions, and demonstrates the practical effectiveness of our proposed algorithm by applying it to a variety of real-world graphical models.

Although $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is isomorphic to the Racah algebra, previous methods failed to establish this isomorphism directly. The emergence of structured testing metrics such as coverage, errors and flaws has sparked interest in new testing techniques that aim to explore complex input spaces of programs with practical implementations. Despite the potential benefits of techniques like paired-permutation testing, there remains a lack of automated tools capable of analyzing paired-permutation testing results for structured metrics. This research fills this gap by introducing a precise automated tool, called PPM Examiner, that explores paired-permutation testing outcomes for structured metrics. The tool's utility is demonstrated through a practical analysis of 200 programs with real-world paired-permutation testing results, showcasing its effectiveness in identifying both genuine issues and false positives.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical anisotropy $\vett{e}$, our results showed that triangular anisotropy $\vett{v}_3$ cannot be directly inferred from the anisotropic geometry of participant spheres, particularly when analyzing Cu+Cu collisions. This discrepancy arises because the anisotropic flow response to anisotropic geometry is not uniformly represented by linear expansion assumptions, particularly for non-central collisions involving triangular anisotropy $\vett{3}$. A deeper understanding of the connection between initial geometry and anisotropic flow requires further analysis of specific collision scenarios, such as central-peripheral and peripheral-peripheral interactions, in order to account for the anisotropic scattering behavior of constituent particles.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are represented on a lattice, and applies it to an extended state representation that includes sensor availability, making decisions about sensor use based on the filter output.

The structure of the ball severely limits how players interact with it, forcing them to be close by, be quick, and use various parts of their bodies in intricate ways.  Despite this constraint, players have developed a vast array of movements and actions on the field, making even the most complex decisions in soccer seemingly instinctive.  However, as players we have limitations, and as a result, determining the best course of action in a given situation is a difficult decision that we leave to coaches, trainers, and in matches, to the players themselves.  Although coaches can guide players on how to play, they cannot provide instantaneous advice on specific decisions.  This is why we believe that creating a system that can instantly provide the best playing strategy for players in various situations would be highly beneficial.  In this study, we propose such a system, which we call an Enhanced Soccer Strategy network, capable of providing the most effective playing approach for players in diverse scenarios.  To achieve this, we designed a new learning algorithm, called the Advantage Actor Critic with an External Policy, and employed a unique policy regularization term to prevent overfitting.  As a result, our proposed model exceeded existing research in various scenarios, demonstrating significant improvements in obtaining the optimal strategy and scoring points in soccer games, indicating its superiority over current methods.

The paper presents a method to utilize a single-component LDV system for acquiring two-dimensional velocity data, despite the limited capability of single-component LDV to measure only instantaneous velocity values at a specific point. This approach involves employing PIV technology to obtain instantaneous two-dimensional velocity maps, which are then used to calculate the frequency spectrum of a fluctuating signal. By doing so, the report demonstrates that single-component LDV can be employed to determine the frequency spectrum of a signal at a specific point, even if PIV measurements might not be sufficient in all situations. The results show that single-component LDV systems can be effectively used to investigate turbulent wake flows behind cylinders, given that PIV is employed to obtain two-dimensional velocity data to begin with.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that combines the Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state.

In experiments involving particle collisions, identifying neutral long-lived particles relies on their decay products. For particles like axions and axion-like spins, decays often produce low-energy photons. Although the Belle II experiment can detect even slim photons, especially when they transform into neutral particles, some scenarios may exclude or displace these particles based on current photon detection limits. We examine the sensitivity of Belle II in detecting or ruling out these particles by analyzing decay products directly, rather than the photons themselves, and draw comparisons with other experiments and future proposals. We also outline an optimization strategy for Belle II to enhance its detection capabilities or lack thereof for these particles.

Recent advances in language models have yielded high performance in text classification tasks, yet the process is complex and largely automated. Our investigation into the semantic alteration detection problem using contextualized language frameworks has several noteworthy findings. First, we discovered that pre-trained language models such as BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT can be effective in identifying semantics changes in text, with BERT demonstrating particularly strong performance. We also found that language models can accurately identify changes in sentiment, sarcasm, and humor in texts, although factors like context and grammar play a crucial role in achieving this outcome. Furthermore, our research revealed that semantics change detection is not significantly enhanced by language models' ability to capture contextual information, although this performance gap closes when evaluating eggXpert's capacity to discern contextually relevant words. Additionally, our findings suggest that semantics change detection is highly correlated with identifying changed words in texts, which can be achieved through language models. We believe that our findings have important implications for developing effective semantics change detection methods and utilizing pre-trained language models in various applications.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), being massive and rotating systems, make ideal detectors for investigating the nature of ultralight pseudoscalars, such as axions and minichams. By examining the spins of black holes at the heart of AGNs, we can determine if these particles have masses below or above an electron mass unit. This research uses a combination of theoretical models and simulation data to analyze the relationship between the pseudoscalar mass and its decay constant, as well as its possible impact on the spinning rate of black holes. A thorough investigation of this phenomenon, specifically the superradiant decay mechanism, requires a deeper understanding of the underlying physical processes, which involves drawing a distinction between the particle's Compton and De Broglie wavelengths. Statistics from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, as well as the 2-10 keV X-ray survey of the 76th SWIFT AGN sample, have yielded insufficient counts of extreme black hole spinning rates that could indicate the presence of ultralight pseudoscalars. Nevertheless, we observe a lack of dancing black holes among low-power AGNs, which may imply that certain AGNs with low spinning rates cannot be explained by the superradiant decay of ultralight pseudoscalars. Therefore, we propose an upper limit for the decay constant of 10^-23 erg/cm, although further research is needed to determine an optimal analysis approach.

Quantum harmonic oscillators with propagation methods have long been studied; our approach uses the path integral representation to calculate the quantum expectations of an oscillator's energy, with its center of mass now experiencing an additional force for simplicity - linear, harmonic, or damping forces. The standard approach to this problem involves the application of DeWitt's functional integral technique, which leads to a second-order partial differential equation that can be solved using the Markov chain Monte Carlo method after some initial conditions are met. A simple harmonic oscillator meets these conditions, allowing the propagation of the quantum oscillator to a new position over time, with the quantum expectations of the oscillator's energy appearing as a constant multiple of the classical expectations. In a harmonic oscillator with propulsive force, even if the quantum effects are negligible, the quantum and classical representations of the oscillator's energy expectations may significantly differ due to the propagation methods used. The two most common approaches to this problem are the stationary phase method and the Gaussian approximation, with the latter leading to the same results as the classical harmonic oscillator for the quantum oscillator's energy expectations. However, the Gaussian approximation has a major limitation: it assumes that the oscillator's wave function is a Gaussian distribution, restricting its application to the harmonic oscillator with propulsive force. On the other hand, the stationary phase method can be applied to any harmonic oscillator with propulsive force but has a flaw: it only works for the quantum oscillator's energy expectations in its ground state. We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare framework to accommodate anticipatory statements, which in turn enables us to incorporate conditional expectations and their applications within the logic.

The integration of solar images by magnetograms and data from vector magnetic field measurements has several applications in solar physics, but it's challenged by the limited coverage and accuracy of existing vector field data.  While errors in photospheric temperature models and measurement biases affect magnetogram images, they're readily quantified and accounted for in data integration methods.  However, the same factors impact vector magnetic field measurement errors, which are currently underestimated due to biases in their calibration data.  These biases affect not only the measurement errors but also how they're estimated and even contribute to data noise.  To address this issue, researchers need to reconsider the calibration process of vector magnetic field measurements or explore alternative methods that bypass it, such as machine learning techniques.  Currently, there's a lack of information on the distribution of these biases for most solar vector magnetic field measurement data, but it's crucial to determine their scope to develop effective correction strategies.  To contribute to this effort, the authors examine the sources of biases in vector magnetic field measurement errors, their impact on data quality, and possible correction approaches.

We establish connections between involutions in groups and boolean structures, introducing a new concept called a "boolean scheme" that serves as the foundation for these connections. A boolean scheme is simply a boolean algebra that has a group structure and is isomorphic to the 2-power set of a set, with its operations corresponding to set intersection and union, as well as the reversible mapping that underlies the inversion of an algebra's involutive operation. We then classify boolean schemes based on their structure, defining a "linear" boolean scheme and its associated linear boolean groups, as well as a "free" boolean scheme and its associated free boolean groups. Furthermore, we explore how these structures relate to linear representations of involutions, particularly in the context of Coxeter graphs and their associated groups, and draw on this knowledge to develop a characterization of boolean graphs that are connected and locally finite, in relation to their own boolean structure.
This research paper confirms that certain types of curves in a 4-dimensional semi-Riemannian space, meeting specific geometric conditions, are actually straight lines.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to select the most suitable one. Despite the importance of this choice, research on loss functions for deep learning still lags behind other aspects, such as model structure and optimization algorithms, in terms of theoretical understanding. This paper seeks to fill this gap by conducting a comprehensive investigation into the effects of loss function modifications for a neural network, focusing on a simple change from cross-entropy loss to quadratic loss as an illustrative example. Our findings reveal that loss function changes can significantly impact both the training and performance of deep learning models, demonstrating that loss functions acting as performance measures often converge during the training process but may not necessarily optimize performance on the target task. Moreover, we observe that loss functions based on the Kullback-Leiber divergence cannot be used directly due to their dependence on a reference distribution, and that loss functions should meet certain conditions to ensure the extraction of useful features. Our research contributes to a deeper understanding of loss functions and their role in deep learning, offering several implications for both theory and practice.

Our proposed atlas, dubbed ATOMIC, is a comprehensive structure of real-world knowledge that comprises if-then statements, whose premises and conclusions have been labeled to facilitate learning models that can draw inferences. Unlike existing datasets that focus on classification, ATOMIC guides the creation of models capable of generating accurate causal links between events, as the statement structure is key to learning such links. We outline a simple algorithm that fills in missing premises and conclusions, obtaining a total of 338,052 if-then statements following various patterns, then further craft a hierarchy within the atlas to develop a multi-task learning approach that integrates inference learning and filling in missing information, resulting in better performance compared to alternative methods and existing datasets.

Our proposed framework uses a dual representation, combining both pixel and spectral information to achieve impressive results in future video forecasting. By leveraging both domains, we've developed a novel pixel-spectral attention mechanism that enhances the model's ability to capture changes and adaptations to lighting conditions. To further improve performance and deal with the increased dimensionality of the combined representation, we've introduced a shared embedding layer for the pixel and spectral domains. Our code has few parameters, reducing the risk of overfitting, and we've designed it to be highly efficient by utilizing a memory-efficient spectral transformation. As a result, we've achieved significant improvements over the current state of the art on two challenging datasets, demonstrating our approach's superiority.

A graph G is said to have a property D if there exists a function McD that assigns a pair of vertices to each non-adjacent pair of vertices in G, such that for any two distinct vertices u and v in G, knowing the pairs of vertices corresponding to all non-adjacent pairs of vertices in G determines whether u and v are adjacent or not. The shortest length at which this property holds true for G is referred to as the metric dimension of G. A graph is said to have a property Sd if there exists a function Mcs that assigns a pair of vertices to each non-adjacent pair of vertices in G, such that for any two distinct vertices u and v in G, knowing the pairs of vertices corresponding to all non-adjacent pairs of vertices at a distance of at most d from u and v determines whether u and v are adjacent or not. The shortest length at which this property holds true for G is referred to as the shortened metric dimension of G.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the subjectivity of expert assessments.  To address this challenge, an automated method is proposed that utilizes deep learning to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds and overcome issues with existing approaches.  A new dataset was created to account for the shortcomings of existing datasets by incorporating various noise sources and a convolutional neural network (CNN) based technique to address the problem of microphone placement variability.  The proposed technique, a combination of a CNN and a long short-term memory (LSTM) network, demonstrates significant improvements in accuracy compared to existing methods and real-world applications.  The proposed technique shows the highest accuracy across all categories in all experiments and demonstrates the effectiveness of CNN-based approaches in overcoming issues with existing methods.  The results suggest that the proposed technique can be an efficient tool for diagnosing heart conditions through cardiac auscultation sounds.

This equilibrium might not hold, especially in low-density molecular gas, which is more susceptible to non-equilibrium conditions.  A lack of excitation equilibrium can lead to inaccurate gas temperatures, which in turn affects our understanding of galaxy evolution, particularly regarding the role of environment in shaping chemical and physical properties of galaxies.
